As a former ‘Big Four’ auditor, I’d be concerned enough to want the evidence behind PwC’s Nvidia sign-off examined closely

PwC signed clean opinions on the accounts and financial reporting controls on 25 February 2026. Its only critical audit matter was “inventory valuation and excess purchase commitments”

Before that sign-off, Singapore had accounted for 22% of quarterly revenue by billing address. Nvidia then switched to customer-headquarters reporting, removing Singapore’s separate line

That change may be legitimate. I’d want to see how PwC established that the disclosures still fairly represented the underlying customer + export risks

Separately, the customer-funding question warrants more than a “shrug”. US audit standards explicitly tell auditors evaluating significant unusual transactions to consider whether counterparties can support the deal without the company’s financial assistance…

I’d want the investment agreements, chip orders, guarantees and side letters examined together: was funding conditional on purchases, could customers meet their obligations, and what risk or control did $NVDA retain?

No revenue “critical audit matter” doesn’t mean no revenue testing... revenue testing is a pre-requisite as becomes a key area of fraud risk but it depends whether the testing they’ve done is “sufficient”

But with an SEC accounting probe now reported, PwC’s risk assessment and the evidence supporting its “clean” opinion deserve serious scrutiny

I’d be sh*tting it if I were the NVDA PwC signing partners… buckle up buttercup I suspect they’ll apportion part of the blame for their legal team to defend if fines come their way!

I covered this earlier in Jan regarding PCB bottlenecks with photonics + $AMZN Kuiper / $SPCX starlink supply chains.

But as an update, it like other industries outside of AI are really starting to feel the pain now too.  

Global Electronics Association: "Is issuing this Industry Alert on escalating shortages across the printed circuit board (PCB) supply chain. 

Companies in automotive, industrial, medical, defense, and telecommunications report longer lead times and difficulty securing supply as AI absorbs scarce capacity, effectively putting production at risk"

The association meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. The association urged buyers to plan ahead for supply constraints and manufacturers.

Hyperscalers like $AMZN already planned ahead of time taking stakes in Gold Circuit Electronics (2368) for supply procurement... 

But can't say the same about other industries procurement (medical industry is probably not used to competing with hyperscalers over the same supply lol). 

The resulting shortages of critical materials, including CCLs and fibreglass cloth, are squeezing supplies for consumer electronics.

TLDR: same bottleneck, same timeline for 2028. It's just interesting to see association warnings about it impacting medical to defense industries. 

So there's incremental information that it's become an industry wide allocation issue. 

I also think it's helpful to see escalating shortages + broadening... so it might show the selloff is starting to look very disconnected with fundamental demand.

$P earnings were actually interesting, not really in terms actionable investments. 

But more on AI capex broadening, where deployments are happening, and what Jensen at $NVDA might envisioned with open weight model + GPU demand. 

- Everpure CEO stated that enterprises are increasingly building on-premises AI factories, stating: 

"The ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront."

- "I'm talking about standard enterprises, regular finance organizations. A wide variety of organizations are starting to buy these AI factories for the purpose of running their own open weight models

From "regular insurance companies, et cetera"

- "One is they're starting to see that these open weight models are actually being able to provide good results, and they're doing so at a fraction of the cost of using the cloud for these workloads"

"that the ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront"

This type of broad industry transition would be heavily bearish as it threatens $ANT, OpenAI and frontier labs over the long term... 

And probably what Jensen saw things heading with $NVDA + additional GPU demand regardless of what frontier lab wins. 

However, I expect more of the open weight effort to collapse or see heavier regulation with how Washington + frontier labs were lobbying. 

- In regards to NAND prices dropping: "If prices come down slowly, I expect to see demand come up along with that" (Jevon) 

- LOL this part was hilarious and the same argument I was using for why qualification cycle players like in optics were so interesting. 

On data center slowdown potential:

"So on the first part of it, remember, I mean, really, the thing that insulates us is we have such a small share going into the hyperscale market"

"even in a down market, they’re going to spend a lot more than our current share amounts to", and their market capture goes up over time relative to overall TAM.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE | NOVEMBER 20 — WEEKLY CLOSE

#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

☢️ Spot uranium held near $90/lb this week. By Friday’s U.S. close, the Sprott Uranium Miners ETF ($URNM) had lost roughly 15% in five sessions. During that same week, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power invited bids for about 13.2 million lb of uranium concentrate for delivery from 2028 through 2037. Bids are due December 28.

🇺🇸 Friday brought the inflation reading I was watching this morning. U.S. households now expect 3.7% inflation over the next year, down a full percentage point from October. Fed Governor Lisa Cook still made the case for higher rates. The Nasdaq fell more than 5% as tech selling intensified after Reuters reported that the SEC was examining Nvidia’s accounting practices.

🥇 Gold was bid near $3,525/oz around 4 p.m. New York time, down roughly 9% from last Friday. 🥈 Silver fell from $48.77 to $40.85 over the same stretch. That’s a 16% loss in a week.

🔶 December copper traded near $5.50/lb on Friday, down from $6.09 a week earlier. Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks rose by 3,204 tonnes to 30,846 tonnes. Even after that increase, those warehouses held less than one day’s worth of Chinese copper consumption.

I remain bullish on uranium. What this week sharpened for me is the financing risk. A developer whose shares fall 15% has to issue nearly 18% more shares to raise the same cash. With utilities already seeking supply through 2037, I’m watching which developers can secure a contract a lender will back and get their mines built in time to deliver.

One problem for crypto is that we’re trying to prove real-world utility while having our best features knee-capped. 
 
The best example is stablecoins, which are fighting for market share while not being allowed to pay interest as a sop to the banking lobby.

Imagine if you could stake tokenized stocks and receive higher dividend payments because you agree to be a long-term shareholder. France does this with paperwork on traditional stocks, but it's complex;crypto could make it easy.  I suspect firms would be lining up for the tokenized stock exemption if they could reward long-term shareholders and work against short-sellers in the new format.
 
We've been so worn down by negotiating in Washington that we've lost some ambition to radically upgrade the system. I understand it, but it's frustrating.

“Ben Graham, my friend and teacher, long ago described the mental attitude toward market fluctuations that I believe to be most conducive to investment success. He said that you should imagine market quotations as coming from a remarkably accommodating fellow named Mr. Market who is your partner in a private business. Without fail, Mr. Market appears daily and names a price at which he will either buy your interest or sell you his. 

Even though the business that the two of you own may have economic characteristics that are stable, Mr. Market's quotations will be anything but. For, sad to say, the poor fellow has incurable emotional problems. At times he feels euphoric and can see only the favorable factors affecting the business. When in that mood, he names a very high buy-sell price because he fears that you will snap up his interest and rob him of imminent gains. At other times he is depressed and can see nothing but trouble ahead for both the business and the world. On these occasions he will name a very low price, since he is terrified that you will unload your interest on him.

Mr. Market has another endearing characteristic: He doesn't mind being ignored. If his quotation is uninteresting to you today, he will be back with a new one tomorrow. Transactions are strictly at your option.

Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you."

- Warren Buffet (1987 Shareholder Letter)

Lots of posts on X that this is 2000, 2008 or 2022.   

At this stage, its not conclusive that we are in a lengthy bear-market. Even those bear-markets had face ripping multi-week rallies and in terms of positioning and sentiment we are very washed out now.

The TMT bust (2000-2002) was triggered by tight monetary which inverted the yield curve and caused a recession. Back then, the NASDAQ also traded at an absurd valuation. Today, the yield curve is not inverted and the NASDAQ's forward PE is at the same level as the COVID-crash low!

The 2008 bust was triggered by the housing bubble and the collapse of various banks; which is not the case today. 

The 2022 bear market was triggered by the Federal Reserve which abruptly ended massive QE and embarked on a severe rate hiking cycle. This is also not similar with the current situation. 

This time around, the market is worrying about a slowdown in AI capex for 2028 and beyond; and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's leadership and circular financing arrangements. In spring the market was also very worried about AI killing cybersecurity and infrastructure software companies and that turned out to be dead wrong. 

The jury is still out on how the Dems sweep will impact the AI capex cycle and how Nvidia's next CEO will manage the business. During times like these when most are super bearish and sentiment is super negative, best to remain calm and focus on the facts.

At this stage, its not conclusive that we are in a lengthy bear-market. Even those bear-markets had face ripping multi-week rallies and in terms of positioning and sentiment we are very washed out now.

The TMT bust (2000-2002) was triggered by tight monetary which inverted the yield curve and caused a recession. Back then, the NASDAQ also traded at an absurd valuation. Today, the yield curve is not inverted and the NASDAQ's forward PE is at the same level as the COVID-crash low!

The 2008 bust was triggered by the housing bubble and the collapse of various banks; which is not the case today. 

The 2022 bear market was triggered by the Federal Reserve which abruptly ended massive QE and embarked on a severe rate hiking cycle. This is also not similar with the current situation. 

This time around, the market is worrying about a slowdown in AI capex for 2028 and beyond; and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's leadership and circular financing arrangements. In spring the market was also very worried about AI killing cybersecurity and infrastructure software companies and that turned out to be dead wrong. 

The jury is still out on how the Dems sweep will impact the AI capex cycle and how Nvidia's next CEO will manage the business. During times like these when most are super bearish and sentiment is super negative, best to remain calm and focus on the facts.

The biggest opportunities right now:

1. build for solving loneliness (the more AI floods everything, the more people crave real human connection, IRL and small social) 

2. build for places with no cameras and no recording (being offline and unseen is turning into the new status symbol)

3. build for the crisis of young men. Millions of guys in their 20s feel completely lost with work, dating, and purpose. Whoever builds real brotherhood, mentorship, and an actual path forward wins a massive market (and helps a ton of people). 

4. build for protecting people's brains (feeds are turning everyone's attention to mush, tools that protect your focus and mood are an easy sell)

5. build for the death of "everyone agrees" (you can find a chart or a podcast clip to prove any point now, people are starving for one source they actually trust)

6. build for day 2, not day 0. Anyone can launch an app in a weekend now. But how can you keep it running, fix the mess, and grow it for 3 years.

7. build for throwaway software (not everything needs to be a $20 a month subscription, tiny apps made for one trip, one wedding, or one group chat are coming)

8. build for people whose ego just got bruised by AI. Millions of smart people are  realizing their job was mostly pattern matching. Help them figure out what they're good for next.

9. build for things that take effort on purpose (when everything is instant and free, nothing feels earned, people will pay for slowness and craft)

10. build for people who miss being told they're wrong. AI agrees with everything you say now. Real rooms where smart people actually push back on your ideas are becoming a luxury.

11. build for skin in the game. The internet is full of free takes and bots. Any platform where people have to put real money, real names, or real work behind what they say wins.

12. build for agents that need to spend money (they're getting virtual cards and budgets, someone builds the spend controls, fraud protection, receipts)

13. build for the end of fake email jobs (half of corporate America knows their job is theater, build the exit ramp for people who want to do real work)

For anyone who’s been keeping up with the streams, you know I put a collar on my Nvidia position on Monday before earnings. 

This was around $155.

I sold the $165 calls for this week and used that premium to buy the $150 puts. The premium covered 77.5% of the cost and I ended up paying a $0.90 debit for the hedge.

I have just exercised those puts and sold my Nvidia position at $150. 

I started buying this name during DeepSeek and ended up getting to an average of $120. Ever since the Jensen news came out, I have felt incredibly uneasy about the position, especially going into earnings given the name couldn’t break out with Jensen on the call so I had no reason to believe it could break out without him.

The risks are simply too high with Nvidia even though the valuation obviously is cheap beyond imagination, assuming the earnings growth continues to be true. The credit backstops, China issues, Jensen not being there…these things could work out but the risk to them at this moment obviously is much higher than normal. The investigation itself is an annoying overhang on the stock regardless of their growth. 

I’ve bagheld various names down and stuck with the story, many times with Nvidia in early 2025, but I was not willing to baghold this name because of Jensen’s affairs. I think the majority of retail are in this name between $120-$140 and now basically have to make a decision if they think things will change or if this company continues forward without Jensen. 

Nvidia can obviously bounce from here, but it’s less about the price action up. It was cheap at $180 and cheap at $150. I wouldn’t care about buying this back at a higher price than I sold, but there would need to be a reason. Just not interested in this until Jensen comes back, if he does.

Importantly, every laser met spec with margin, which matters a lot more in production than one device achieving extraordinary performance.
